title: Natural selection reduces superfluous parts without compensatory enlargement

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Natural selection reduces superfluous parts without compensatory enlargement

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Natural selection will in the long run reduce any part of the organisation once it becomes superfluous, saving nutriment, without necessarily causing another part to enlarge; and it can enlarge an organ without requiring reduction of an adjoining part.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Thus, as I believe, natural selection will always succeed in the long run in reducing and saving every part of the organisation, as soon as it is rendered superfluous, without by any means causing some other part to be largely developed in a corresponding degree.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Compensation and economy of growth.”. Scope: all organisms, e.g. parasitic cirripedes losing the carapace

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Comparative anatomy can test organ reduction and compensation in well-studied transitions. The universal, long-run causal claim exceeds existing functional and historical data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify repeated transitions in which an organ became functionally superfluous and reconstruct its size, energetic cost and correlated changes in other parts. Consistent reduction without obligatory compensatory enlargement supports the claim; persistent superfluous organs or mandatory compensation refute its universal form.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Functional superfluity and historical selection are difficult to establish.

Energetic costs and compensatory growth are rarely recorded with morphology.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.57
discriminating power: 0.43
analysis feasibility: 0.51
operationalizability: 0.54
data adequacy: 0.37

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Compensation versus independent reduction can be compared in birds with reduced wings and in a few genetic models of trait loss. Superfluous is not an independent measurement in those tables, which lowers the force of a positive result. The anti-necessity wording is easier to support, with single well-measured counterexamples to obligatory trade-offs, than the claim that selection always removes every superfluous part.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On phylogenies, score reduction of structures that have lost their function and ask whether a neighbouring structure enlarges in compensation. Reduction without obligatory enlargement would support the economy clause; enlargement that always requires reduction of an adjoining part would refute that clause. The always-reduced clause would be refuted by functionless structures that are retained without a detectable cost.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Gene loss and morphological compensation are rarely measured in the same species.

Superfluous is often inferred from the reduction, which circularly supports the claim.

Allometry creates apparent trade-offs that are not nutritional compensation.
